title: Subject-verb agreement
lede: A verb has to match its subject. The rule takes ten seconds to learn. Finding the real subject is the skill, and this lesson trains it.

sections.md:
## The rule
A **singular subject** takes a **singular verb**. A **plural subject** takes a **plural verb**.

- The truck **runs**. The trucks **run**.
- She **is** ready. They **are** ready.

Careful: in the present tense, the **singular** verb is the one that ends in *-s*. Nouns work the opposite way. *The driver drives. The drivers drive.* One *-s* per pair, never two.

Nobody gets this wrong in short sentences. The mistakes happen when the subject is **hidden**, **split** or **disguised**. Every section below is one of those disguises.

## Disguise 1: words in between
The verb agrees with the **subject**, not with the noun closest to it.

- The **list** of overdue invoices **is** on your desk. (*list is*, not *invoices are*)
- The **cost** of the new tires **was** higher than expected.

**Method:** cross out every prepositional phrase (*of the invoices*, *in the yard*, *with the drivers*). What's left is the subject.

Phrases like **along with**, **as well as**, **together with** and **in addition to** don't add to the subject. They're just extra information.

- The **manager**, along with two dispatchers, **was** at the meeting.

sections.q: Choose the verb: "The **box** of brake pads ___ in the shop."
sections.why: Cross out *of brake pads*. **The box is.**

sections.md:
## Disguise 2: compound subjects
- **And** joins subjects into a plural: *The driver **and** the dispatcher **are** on the call.*
- **Or** and **nor** don't add. The verb agrees with whichever subject is **closer** to it: *Neither the manager nor the **drivers were** told.* *Neither the drivers nor the **manager was** told.*

The second sentence is correct but sounds odd. When that happens, put the plural subject last. It reads better.

## Disguise 3: indefinite pronouns
| Always singular | Always plural | Depends on the noun after *of* |
|---|---|---|
| each, every, either, neither, everyone, everybody, anyone, someone, no one, nobody, everything, nothing | both, few, many, several, others | **some, any, none, all, most** |

- **Each** of the trucks **has** a GPS.
- **Several** of the trucks **have** dash cams.
- **Some** of the **money is** missing. **Some** of the **trucks are** late.

*None* used to be treated as always singular. Today both *none is* and *none are* are standard. Use *none is* when you mean "not one" and *none are* when you mean "not any of them."

sections.q: "Every one of the drivers ___ a clean record."
sections.why: The subject is **every one**, which is singular. *Of the drivers* is crossed out.

sections.md:
## Disguise 4: the subject comes after the verb
In sentences starting with **There** or **Here**, the real subject comes **after** the verb.

- There **are** three loads waiting. (*loads are*)
- There **is** a problem with the invoice. (*problem is*)
- Here **come** the inspectors.

In speech, people say *there's* for everything ("there's three loads"). In writing, flip the sentence in your head: *Three loads are there.*

## Disguise 5: words that look plural or singular but aren't
- **Collective nouns** (team, company, jury, family, staff) are **singular** in American English when the group acts as one unit: *The company **is** expanding.* (British English often says *the company are*.)
- **Amounts treated as one unit** are singular: *Ten thousand dollars **is** a lot. Five miles **is** a long run.*
- **Nouns ending in -s that are singular:** news, economics, mathematics, physics, measles. *The news **is** bad.*
- **The number of** = singular. **A number of** = plural. *The number of complaints **is** rising. A number of drivers **have** quit.*
- **Titles** are singular: *"Trading in the Zone" **is** on my list.*

sections.title: Untangle a long sentence
sections.problem: "The results of the safety inspection, which covered every truck in the fleet, ___ due Friday."
steps: Cross out the *which* clause: it's extra information.

sections.title: Linking verbs
steps: With *is/are* in the middle, the verb agrees with the **subject** (before it), not the word after it.
sections.answer: **is**. *The biggest problem is the brakes.* Flip it and it changes: *The brakes are the biggest problem.*

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Each** after a plural subject doesn't make it singular: *The drivers **each** have a key.* (Subject: *drivers*.)
- **Data** is technically plural (one *datum*), and scientists often still write *the data are*. In everyday and business writing, *the data is* is standard. Pick one and stay consistent.
- **Who, which, that** take the number of the word they point to. That leads to the hardest agreement question in English. It's in the challenge questions below.

practice.q: "The stack of invoices ___ on the desk."
"The driver and his partner ___ on the road by 5 AM."
"Either the drivers or the dispatcher ___ to blame."
practice.why: With **or**, the verb agrees with the closer subject: *dispatcher is*.

practice.q: "Each of the new trucks ___ a sleeper cab."
"There ___ two loads left in the yard."
practice.why: The subject comes after the verb: *two loads are*.
**News** is singular even though it ends in *-s*.

practice.q: "A number of drivers ___ asked for the weekend off."
practice.why: **A number of** = several = plural. *The number of* would be singular.
**Most** depends on the noun after *of*. *Fuel* can't be counted, so it's singular.

practice.q: "He is one of those drivers who ___ never late."
practice.why: **Who** points to *drivers* (there's a group of drivers who are never late, and he's one of them), so *who are*.
practice.hint: Ask: which word does *who* point back to, *one* or *drivers*?

practice.q: "He is the only one of the drivers who ___ never late."
practice.why: Now **who** points to *the only one*: only one person is never late. So *who is*. One word, *only*, flips the verb.
practice.hint: Compare with the previous question. Who exactly is never late here?

practice.q: "The CEO, as well as the board members, ___ against the merger."
practice.why: **As well as** doesn't make a compound subject. Cross it out: *The CEO is against the merger.*
practice.hint: Is *as well as* the same as *and*?

options: Neither of the offers are good enough.
The team have won three straight games. (American English)
Twenty dollars is too much for that.
There's three trucks in the shop.
practice.why: An **amount treated as one sum** is singular. *Neither* is singular (*neither is*). American English treats *team* as singular. *There are three trucks.*
practice.hint: Three of these break a rule from this lesson. Check each against a disguise.
